# Kīṭāgiri Sutta (MN 70 (PTS MN i 473))

**ID:** MN 70 (PTS MN i 473)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kīṭāgiri Sutta* (MN 70) is set at Kīṭāgiri and addresses the health benefits of restricting meals to one part of the day, as well as the reluctance of certain mendicants to accept this training [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2017]. In the narrative framing, a group of unruly monastics—identified in tradition as the "group of six" (*chabbhaggiya*)—flouted the meal regulations, maintaining that they felt healthy and at ease eating at all times of the day [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2017]. In response, the Buddha explains that bodily and mental feelings (pleasant, painful, or neutral) cannot be judged solely by their affective tone; instead, the decisive spiritual criterion is whether a given feeling leads to the increase of wholesome states and the decrease of unwholesome states [Anālayo 2014; Anālayo 2017].

The sutta is also celebrated for presenting a fundamental typology of seven noble persons (*ariya-puggalā*): the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), the one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*), the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*), the one attained to view (*diṭṭhippatta*), the one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*), the Dhamma-follower (*dhammānusārī*), and the faith-follower (*saddhānusārī*) [Galasek 2016]. In defining these categories, the text explains that the arahant "liberated by wisdom" destroys all taints without directly experiencing the peaceful formless deliverances with the body, whereas the "liberated in both ways" attains both [Bodhi 1984; Hung 2010; Wen]. Persons at lower stages, such as the body-witness, touch the formless deliverances bodily while having only partially destroyed their defilements [Jantrasrisalai 2008; Bodhi 2012].

  In Pali-internal text reuse, DharmaNexus identifies 3,903 matching passages across 162 Pali texts, sharing the largest blocks of text with the *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* (MN 85, §21.7–21.8 ↔ §59.1–59.2), the *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), and the *Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta* (MN 114) [DharmaNexus]. It is also aligned by DharmaNexus with passages in the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi* and texts in the Tibetan Kangyur [DharmaNexus].
